title: 3-Read Friday #3: Explaining vs Demonstrating, Checking for Listening, and Productive Struggle
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Issue three gathers three posts on how students actually take in and process instruction. Barton opens with Andrew Watson's write-up of a study comparing whether it's more effective to show learners how to do something or tell them, a question Barton says he found genuinely surprising in its results. He then covers Nick Wood's confidence-based "check for listening" technique, where students hold up 1 to 5 fingers to signal how sure they are of an answer, which Barton connects to his own upcoming podcast on securing student attention. He closes with Greg Ashman's post on productive struggle, which reviews a study linking the "struggle" model to maths anxiety — a topic Barton says he has "long wrestled with" given how often lower-confidence students simply give up rather than persist. All three items are squarely about instructional technique grounded in research, making this one of the more clearly Learning & Curriculum issues in the early run.
points: Barton highlights that the "show vs. tell" research produced a surprising result, and credits Watson with drawing out the implications for how teachers should plan explanations.
He connects Wood's finger-based confidence check directly to his own preparation for a podcast on securing student attention, showing the idea influencing his near-term work.
He flags Ashman's post as confronting his own long-held ambivalence about "productive struggle," specifically its link to maths anxiety in less confident students.
quotes: This post cites a fascinating study about whether it is best to show people how to do something, or tell them how to do something.
What I really like is the way Andrew draws out important implications for teachers planning their own explanations.
Nick has been experimenting by asking his students to indicate how confident they feel about an answer by holding up their fingers: 1 finger is not at all confident, 5 fingers is very confident.

I have long wrestled with the idea of productive struggle. It sounds logical: create conditions where students struggle with a problem, and students should develop greater resilience and (somehow) greater conceptual understanding.
This post by Greg looks at a recent study that investigated the effect of productive struggle on maths anxiety.
